A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GIOROM and contain readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The substantial revisions and relocated material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: V1 reports original physical simulations, prediction errors, inference timings, and ablation results in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: V2 reports original simulation results, ROM reconstruction comparisons, neural-solver benchmarks, and architecture and sampling ablations.

M1.justification: V2 replaces v1's Fourier neural operator processor with a neural operator transformer using heterogeneous attention, adopts farthest-point sampling, and adds a position-reconstruction term to the acceleration loss. These change the procedure substantially. The regrouping of message passing and GNO layers under the Interaction Operator name is largely organizational.

E1.justification: Coverage narrows within the retained six material families. V2 Appendix E no longer lists v1's separate SPH Water-3D dataset or NCLAW-generated Jelly trajectories, and reduces granular datasets from three to two. Both versions retain 2D and 3D physics; v2 still explicitly mentions Goop-3D.

E2.justification: V2 adds POD and autoencoder reconstruction comparisons and GNOT and IPOT time-stepper baselines. V1's standalone FNO and MeshGraphNet benchmark comparisons disappear, although FNO-based architectures remain in v2's ablations. GNS is retained, appearing as GNN in v2 Table 4 and GNS in Table 7.

E3.justification: Reported training increases from 1 million to 5 million steps, validation expands from five to ten held-out sets per material, and noise settings and trajectory counts and lengths change. V2 Table 4 evaluates baselines on reduced-order systems, whereas v1's principal accuracy comparison concerns full-order performance. These are substantive protocol revisions, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds ROM index-randomization tests, transformer and interaction-operator component ablations, interchangeable time-stepper comparisons, and random/FPS versus radius/Delaunay graph tests. It revises sparsity and noise analyses and replaces FNO-specific hyperparameter studies with transformer studies. Existing viscosity and several sensitivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: V2 Table 3 explicitly reports three index-randomization retries for each reconstruction method, adding repeat-level reporting absent from v1. This does not establish repeated model training or additional training seeds. Neither version provides confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Benchmark errors are extensively replaced, and reconstruction, component, and sampling results are added. V2 Table 4 places GNN ahead of GIOROM on Sand-3D, at 0.0008 versus 0.0009 rollout MSE. Listed runtime for 200 steps on 1776 particles changes from 4.4 seconds to 3.9 seconds. Changed architectures and protocols prevent interpreting the revised accuracy numbers as same-setting gains.

T1.justification: V2 substantially expands the mathematical specification of the simulated physics: Section 5.1 introduces an elastodynamic governing equation, and Appendix E adds constitutive, energy, stress, and yield formulations for the material systems. V1's explicit FNO spectral-convolution equations are removed. The core GNO and least-squares ROM mathematics remains, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions shift from a novel GINO-enhancing interaction operator and a 25-fold speedup claim to a broader sampling-based ROM framework, a transformer time-stepper, and a claimed 6.6–32-fold input reduction. Discretization invariance and arbitrary spatial reconstruction remain central, but the stated contribution and quantitative headline are substantially redefined.

C2.justification: V2 introduces explanations linking attention to reduced dependence on training noise, discusses alternative time-steppers, and interprets neural fields primarily as an inference-speed mechanism. It also identifies degradation under extreme sparsity and qualifies geometry generalization. V1's general noise-sensitivity limitation becomes a material-dependent discussion; the extreme-distribution-shift and discontinuity limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds boundary-feature formulas, physical boundary conditions and time increments, neural-field training-loss details, and expanded material-generation specifications. It revises architecture settings and documents Adamax with weight decay instead of Adam. These substantially change reproducibility information, although newly stated physical details do not alone prove changed simulations. The code-access link remains unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 substantially develops positioning against intrusive continuous ROMs requiring known PDEs and discretization-specific POD/autoencoders, shifting emphasis from v1's GINO augmentation. It adds references including Hao et al. (2023), Lusch et al. (2018), and Smith et al. (2018), while removing several numerical-method references. Much of the general related-work survey is retained.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. Problem-setting mathematics moves into the introduction, the method is reorganized around spatial reduction and temporal dynamics, and results and baselines become experiment subsections followed by a new discussion structure. Appendix organization, terminology, citation style, and the expansion of GIOROM also change.

P2.justification: The architecture diagram is redrawn, Figure 2 changes from visual baseline comparisons to material rollout sequences, and Figure 3 expands to include FPS and Delaunay graphs. V1 Figures 4 and 8 are combined in v2 Figure 4. Benchmark tables and ablation plots are extensively restructured, while several existing displays are relocated.

improvement.justification: V2 improves scientific assessability through direct ROM comparisons, targeted component and sampling tests, and clearer separation of full-order and reduced-order results. These provide better support for design choices than v1. The gain is limited by removal of the earlier full-order baseline accuracy comparisons and inconsistent documentation: Equation 10 adds a position loss that Algorithm 2 omits. Lower errors under revised training and evaluation settings do not independently establish improvement.
